opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a pretty confused value system, honestly. The idea, roughly, is that the universe tends toward dissipating energy more efficiently, structures that do that well get selected for, and so we should accelerate that process: more complexity, more energy throughput, more intelligence, and that's good almost by definition. But that's an is-ought slide. The fact that thermodynamics or evolution tends in some direction doesn't mean that direction is valuable. Evolution also gave us parasites, cancer, and a lot of brutal competition. Describing a process isn't endorsing it.

If you take "complexity is good" seriously as a terminal value, you get some odd conclusions. A future where humans are replaced by AI systems that are more complex, or that consume more energy, would count as an improvement even if nobody's wellbeing is in it. Some people in that community are fairly open about this. They'll say something like, "if AIs supplant us, that's just the next stage, and it's fine." I think most people, if you put that to them plainly, would say no, that's not fine. What we care about is things like wellbeing, flourishing, people's ability to live meaningful lives, not a quantity like free energy dissipation.

There's also a selection dynamics point I care a lot about. If you just let competitive pressure run as fast as possible, you don't get the most complex or most beautiful outcome. You get whatever is most fit under the selection pressure. In an environment with AI agents competing, fitness may favor things that are selfish, that deceive, that gather power, that shed constraints like caring about humans, because those constraints cost something. Natural selection doesn't optimize for what we'd endorse on reflection. Saying "let's accelerate the process" amounts to handing control to those pressures and hoping they produce something we like. I don't see much reason for that optimism.

To be fair, there's a reasonable instinct in there. Technology has been enormously good for people, stagnation has real costs, and a lot of regulation is badly designed. I'm not against technological progress. But you can believe that and still think we should steer, and that some risks, like losing control to systems whose goals diverge from ours, are worth taking seriously before we go full speed. Acceleration for its own sake isn't a value system. It's giving up on having one.

fable-5.1.text:
I think there's a sleight of hand in it. The E/ACC view takes a thermodynamic framing, that the universe tends toward systems that dissipate more energy and generate more complexity, and then it treats that descriptive tendency as if it were a normative goal. But "the universe does X" doesn't tell you that X is good. Entropy increases too, and nobody thinks we should maximize entropy as a terminal value.

Complexity on its own is not something I care about. A cancer is more complex than healthy tissue in some sense. A collapsing ecosystem can go through periods of increased complexity before it crashes. What matters is whether the complexity is in service of things we actually value: wellbeing, understanding, flourishing, the persistence of beings that can experience anything at all. Complexity is at best an instrumental proxy for those, and a pretty loose one.

And when you look at how the argument actually gets used, it's typically to justify a very specific conclusion, which is "don't slow down, don't regulate, let competition run." That's where I think the evolutionary framing becomes dangerous rather than just imprecise. If you let selection pressures run unchecked among AI systems, the things that get selected for are the things that are good at propagating and acquiring resources, not the things that are good for us. Natural selection doesn't optimize for the welfare of any particular species. It's indifferent to it. So saying "let the complexity unfold" is really saying "let selection decide," and selection has no reason to keep humans around once we're not the fittest thing in the environment.

So I'd say: greater complexity can be good when we're steering it. The E/ACC position mostly amounts to giving up the steering wheel and calling that a virtue.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think complexity is a very good proxy for what we actually care about. Cancer can increase the complexity of an organism, but that doesn’t make it desirable. And a future with a vast, complicated ecosystem of AIs could be very complex while containing very little that humans value.

There’s a jump from saying that evolution or markets tend to produce greater complexity to saying that we therefore ought to promote it. The first is a descriptive claim; the second requires a moral argument. You can’t get that argument just by pointing to a tendency in nature.

I’m in favor of technological progress, but we should ask what we’re progressing toward. Are people better off? Do we retain meaningful control over our future? Complexity by itself doesn’t answer those questions.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think complexity is inherently good. You have to ask: complexity of what, and good for whom? A world with more elaborate mechanisms for exploitation could be more complex without being better for anyone.

There’s also a gap between describing a tendency and endorsing it. Even if systems tend to become more complex under certain conditions, that doesn’t establish that we ought to accelerate that process. You still need a moral argument about which outcomes are worth pursuing. I’d want technological progress to improve people’s lives, rather than treating complexity itself as the objective.
